title: Hands-Only CPR
hook: If an adult collapses and isn't breathing, you don't need training certificates or rescue breaths — just two steps that can double or triple their chance of survival.
key_points: For a sudden adult collapse, hands-only CPR is recommended for untrained bystanders.
Step 1: call emergency services (or have someone else call).
Step 2: push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about 100–120 pushes a minute.
Keep going until help or an AED arrives — doing something beats doing nothing.
content_html: Cardiac arrest can strike without warning, and survival drops with every minute that passes. The American Heart Association's hands-only CPR strips lifesaving down to something any bystander can do — no mouth-to-mouth, no certification required.
extra_html: For a teen or adult who suddenly collapses, the AHA recommends hands-only CPR for untrained or uncertain bystanders, and it comes down to two steps. First, call emergency services immediately — or, better, point to a specific person and tell them to call and to find an AED. Second, place the heel of one hand in the center of the chest, your other hand on top, and push hard and fast — about two inches deep, at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute (the tempo of "Stayin' Alive"). Don't stop to check or hesitate; keep compressions going until emergency responders or an automated external defibrillator arrives. The AHA's central message is reassuring: imperfect CPR vastly beats none, and a bystander willing to push on the chest can be the difference between life and death.

related.title: Treating Minor Cuts and Burns
related.hook: Most household cuts and burns heal fine with the right first move — and knowing the few that need a doctor keeps a small injury from becoming a big one.

related.title: When a Symptom Needs a Doctor
related.hook: Most everyday symptoms pass on their own. The skill worth having is recognizing the red flags that mean don't wait — call for help now.

flashcards.prompt: What are the two steps of hands-only CPR?
flashcards.back_html: 1. Call emergency services (or have someone call). 2. Push hard and fast in the center of the chest until help arrives.

flashcards.prompt: How fast should you push during hands-only CPR?
flashcards.explanation_html: The AHA recommends chest compressions at a rate of 100–120 per minute — roughly the beat of the song 'Stayin' Alive'.
